	The genesis for these arguments could go all the way back to the Bible
(Cain/Abel) or Plato (Phaedrus) but are much more common starting about 1740 
or so.  German philosophers, in particular, covered this ground again and again
and again.  Also, in Russia, Tolstoy and Dostoevski extensively covered this
ground.  Dostoevski's Notes from Underground is in fact the autobiography of TK
written 130 years before the fact.  Tolstoy said: "As technology increases,
individual freedom decreases."  Gad, these truths are so old! 
	The manifesto is all over the place: download, read, read some more, and good
luck.
		Ehrlich

	He regards a physical constraint on what a person can accomplish as
a fact of nature to be endured or got around.  The fact that one cannot walk
100 miles in a day for example.  He regards a social constraint -- the fact
that one can't get material goods without working at a job -- as unendurable.

appropriate only when the constraint is perceived as arbitrary and/or caused by
someone else violating norms.

	Here is a rule of thumb for the identification of surrogate activities.  Given
a person who devotes much time and energy to the pursuit of goal 
X, ask yourself this: If he had to devote most of his time and energy to 
satisfying his biological needs, and if that effort required him to use his
physical and mental facilities in a varied and interesting way, would he feel
seriously deprived because he did not attain goal X? If the answer is no, then
the person's pursuit of a goal X is a surrogate activity.   
		Industrial Society And Its Future, by ���FC��� (para 39)
